clinicalPearls: Caused by a heteroplasmic point mutation in mitochondrial DNA, classically m.3243A>G in MT-TL1; inheritance is strictly maternal with no male-to-offspring transmission.
Sensorineural hearing loss is typically bilateral and high-frequency and often precedes the onset of diabetes by years.
Diabetes results from progressive beta-cell failure rather than insulin resistance; patients are usually lean and may transition from oral agents to insulin over time.
A macular pattern dystrophy with perifoveal retinal pigment change is characteristic and often spares central vision early on.
The same mutation underlies MELAS, so remain alert to overlapping features such as stroke-like episodes, myopathy and raised lactate.
Metformin is generally avoided because of the theoretical risk of precipitating lactic acidosis in mitochondrial disease.
Systemic involvement may include cardiomyopathy, renal disease with a focal segmental glomerulosclerosis picture, and short stature.
Heteroplasmy level and its tissue distribution largely determine severity and the spectrum of organ involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder arises from a heteroplasmic pathogenic variant in mitochondrial DNA, most commonly m.3243A>G within MT-TL1, the gene encoding the mitochondrial transfer RNA for leucine (UUR). Impaired mitochondrial tRNA function disrupts intramitochondrial protein synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation, so tissues with high metabolic demand — pancreatic beta cells, the cochlea, the retina, myocardium, skeletal muscle and kidney — are preferentially affected. Because mitochondria are transmitted exclusively through the oocyte, inheritance is maternal, and the proportion of mutant to wild-type genomes (heteroplasmy) within a given tissue, together with a threshold effect, explains both the wide phenotypic variability and the shared genetic basis with MELAS.
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing for m.3243A>G, preferably on urinary epithelial cells or buccal mucosa rather than blood
Dilated fundoscopy with optical coherence tomography for pattern dystrophy
Renal function and urinalysis for proteinuria
Islet autoantibodies, expected to be negative
redFlags: New or progressive cardiomyopathy and heart failure
Declining renal function or nephrotic-range proteinuria
reference.prognosis: A chronic, progressive multisystem disorder in which outcome depends on heteroplasmy and the organs involved. Cardiac and renal complications are the main determinants of premature mortality.
pitfalls: Frequently mislabelled as type 1 or type 2 diabetes, delaying recognition of the maternal pedigree and associated deafness.
Blood testing may miss the mutation because leucocyte heteroplasmy declines with age, so urinary sediment is the preferred sample.
Islet autoantibodies are negative, which should reinforce rather than exclude the diagnosis in the right context.
The risk of provoking lactic acidosis with certain oral agents is easily overlooked in day-to-day management.
management: Treat the diabetes as progressive beta-cell failure, favouring early insulin, while avoiding metformin because of the lactic-acidosis risk in mitochondrial disease
Hearing rehabilitation with hearing aids, and cochlear implantation for advanced sensorineural hearing loss
Consider coenzyme Q10 supplementation and avoid mitochondrial-toxic drugs such as aminoglycosides
Regular retinal review for the macular pattern dystrophy
Cardiac surveillance with echocardiography for cardiomyopathy and renal monitoring for proteinuria and nephropathy, the main determinants of prognosis
Remain alert to MELAS-overlap features such as stroke-like episodes, myopathy and lactic acidosis
Genetic counselling explaining strictly maternal inheritance with variable heteroplasmy, offering family screening
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across endocrinology, audiology, ophthalmology, cardiology and genetics
